Session 2 · 2.1 Why architecture is a business topicBook ↗

Architecture is the set of decisions that are expensive to change

  • What the major parts are, what each does, how they talk
  • Cost: a few dollars a month or tens of thousands
  • Risk: what happens when a component fails; how a breach could occur
  • Speed: how fast features ship without breaking what works
The person who cannot follow the conversation does not get a vote.
Session 2 · 2.2 Clients, servers, and programs · 1/2Book ↗

One computer asks, another answers

  • Client asks; server waits and answers. The client always speaks first
  • A server is an ordinary computer in a data center, running 24 hours a day
Session 2 · 2.2 Clients, servers, and programs · 2/2Book ↗

Two things people get wrong about servers

  • A server is an ordinary computer: processor, memory, disk. Usually no screen
  • "Server" also names a program: a web server program listens for requests and hands back pages
  • The client for a website is a browser: Chrome, Safari, Firefox, Edge
  • Analogy: the restaurant. You order from the menu; the kitchen cooks; you never enter the kitchen
Session 2 · 2.3 A web page is three languages · 1/3Book ↗

A web page is a plain text file

  • HTML: what is on the page (headings, paragraphs, images, links), marked with tags
  • CSS: what it looks like (colors, fonts, layout, phone versus desktop)
  • JavaScript: what it does (react to clicks, validate forms, load more posts)
  • JavaScript is unrelated to Java despite the name
Session 2 · 2.3 A web page is three languages · 2/3Book ↗

HTML by example

<h1>Rosenthal's Bakery</h1>
<p>Fresh bread every morning since 1998.</p>
<img src="storefront.jpg" alt="Our shop">
<a href="menu.html">See the menu</a>
  • Read it aloud and it explains itself: heading, paragraph, image, link
Session 2 · 2.3 A web page is three languages · 3/3Book ↗

Three files, one page

  • The browser combines all three and renders the result
Session 2 · 2.4 The static website on your own computerBook ↗

The zero-infrastructure starting point

  • A static website is fixed files sent to every visitor exactly as stored
  • Double-click index.html: the browser reads it straight off your disk. Address starts with file:///
  • No server, no internet, no company involved
  • Limitation: only you can see it. Sharing needs an always-on server with an address
Session 2 · 2.5 How the internet delivers a page · 1/5Book ↗

Anatomy of a URL

  • Protocol (how to talk), domain (which server), path (which page), query string (extra details)
Session 2 · 2.5 How the internet delivers a page · 2/5Book ↗

Finding the server: DNS

  • Every machine on the internet has a numeric IP address, such as 142.250.72.14
  • DNS is the distributed phone book: domain name in, IP address out
  • A business rents its domain from a registrar; pointing it at a host means editing a DNS record
  • "DNS changes take up to 48 hours": thousands of copies of the phone book refresh on a schedule
Session 2 · 2.5 How the internet delivers a page · 3/5Book ↗

The conversation: HTTP

GET /menu.html HTTP/1.1
Host: www.rosenthalsbakery.com
User-Agent: Chrome/128.0

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html

<!DOCTYPE html> ...
  • A request names a method and a path plus headers; a response carries a status code and the content
  • 200 OK, 301 moved, 404 not found, 500 server error, 503 overloaded
Session 2 · 2.5 How the internet delivers a page · 4/5Book ↗

What happens after you press Enter

  • One page usually means 50 to 150 requests: HTML first, then CSS, JavaScript, images
Session 2 · 2.5 How the internet delivers a page · 5/5Book ↗

HTTPS and hosting

  • Plain HTTP is readable by anyone on the same Wi-Fi. HTTPS wraps it in encryption; the padlock
  • The server proves its identity with a free certificate. No business reason to skip HTTPS
  • Hosting: rent space on someone's always-on server. Static hosting is free or nearly so
  • Serving static files is the easiest job a computer can do: fast, hard to hack, hard to overload
Session 2 · 2.6 Front end, back end, and the limits of static · 1/2Book ↗

What a static site cannot do

  • Front end: runs on the user's device. Back end: runs on the server, out of sight
  • A static site is front end only, so it cannot: remember anything, personalise, keep a secret, or do work (email, charge a card)
  • A dynamic website runs a program per request and can do all four
Session 2 · 2.6 Front end, back end, and the limits of static · 2/2Book ↗

Static versus dynamic

  • Most real products mix the two: static marketing pages, dynamic product behind the login
Session 2 · 2.7 Where Python fitsBook ↗

Python runs on the server, not in the browser

LanguageWhere it runsJob
HTML, CSSBrowserContent and appearance
JavaScriptBrowser (and servers via Node.js)Interactivity; also back ends
PythonServers and your own computerBack-end logic, data, AI, scripts
SQLDatabase serverQuestions about stored data
Swift, KotlinPhonesNative apps
Your Python skills are directly the skills of writing back ends. "What's your stack?" means "what's your architecture?"
